notes.meaning: Solomon decides to run an experiment by chasing after fun and earthly pleasures to see if they can bring true happiness. He speaks directly to his own heart, giving himself permission to enjoy every good thing around him. Yet as soon as he tests this way of life, he finds that pleasure is empty and cannot satisfy the human soul.

Wild laughter and constant parties cannot heal a hurting heart or quiet a guilty conscience. Solomon calls loud, unrestrained joking a kind of madness because it blinds people to what really matters. When the party ends, earthly pleasure leaves a person just as empty as before.

Next, Solomon tests fine food and wine, while deliberately keeping his mind sharp and observant. He does not become a reckless drunkard; instead, he uses wisdom to steer his thoughts like a driver holding the reins. He wants to know if earthly comforts can give people real purpose during their short lives on earth.

Turning from simple party-going to royal projects, Solomon throws himself into building fine palaces and planting sprawling vineyards. These huge works gave him creative joy and put his wealth and royal status on display. Yet even these grand achievements were done mainly to please himself.

Solomon designs magnificent walled gardens, orchards, and parks filled with all kinds of fruit trees. His deep study of plants helped him create lush, beautiful landscapes that felt like personal paradises. He hoped surrounding himself with natural beauty would finally fill the emptiness inside him.

To keep his vast gardens and thick groves of trees green in a dry land, he builds giant stone reservoirs and aqueducts. These waterworks required brilliant engineering and massive effort to channel water where it was needed. They stood as lasting monuments to his skill and power.

A king with such huge estates needed a massive workforce, so Solomon buys many servants and has whole families born in his royal household. He also gathers enormous herds of cattle and flocks of sheep, far exceeding anyone who ruled Jerusalem before him. His daily court was famous for its unmatched size, splendor, and food supplies.

Tribute and taxes poured in from neighboring rulers, filling Solomon's storehouses with silver, gold, and rare treasures. He brought in male and female singers for royal entertainment and gathered many women into his harem. He had access to every luxury and delight known to kings.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the rare Hebrew words at the end of the verse are difficult to translate; while many ancient versions suggested musical instruments or cup-bearers, the context of royal luxury strongly supports concubines or ladies of the harem.

notes.meaning: Solomon became greater and wealthier than all previous kings, yet he still maintained his keen intellectual powers. God allowed him to keep his ability to think critically and weigh his experiences. He was not blinded by his luxuries; he watched and judged everything he did.

Whenever Solomon saw something he wanted, he had the wealth and power to take it without hesitation. He experienced genuine, temporary satisfaction while accomplishing his great building and creative tasks. That momentary thrill of success was the only real reward his hard labor could give him.

When Solomon steps back to examine the total result of his life's work, the feeling of satisfaction completely vanishes. He realizes that everything he made was like chasing the wind, offering no lasting profit or peace. Without a connection to God and eternity, earthly success leaves a person empty.

Solomon turns back to compare wisdom with foolish living, knowing his findings are final and complete. No future king could ever possess greater wealth, power, or opportunity to test life's pleasures than he had. Anyone who comes after him will only repeat the same experiment and reach the same conclusion.

Even though wisdom cannot solve every mystery of life, Solomon admits it is far better than folly. Just as bright daylight is superior to pitch darkness, a clear and thoughtful mind helps a person navigate daily life. Wisdom preserves dignity and prevents many foolish mistakes.

A wise man walks with his eyes open, seeing dangers ahead and steering his life with good sense, while a fool blindly stumbles into trouble. Yet, despite this great advantage during life, Solomon sees a harsh reality that levels both men. The exact same end—physical death—catches up with the wise man and the fool alike.

Solomon applies this bitter truth to himself, realizing that all his brilliant intellect cannot save him from the grave. If he must die just like a fool, he questions what earthly benefit his great wisdom actually gave him. Looking at life purely from a worldly point of view, he concludes that even human wisdom is futile.

Earthly fame does not last, and coming generations soon forget both the wise thinker and the ignorant fool. Time sweeps away the memory of ordinary mortals, burying their achievements in silence. Solomon laments that death makes no distinction between the learned and the foolish.

Looking at life strictly from an earthly angle, Solomon finds himself hating life because all human effort seems so heavy and pointless. Everything men do under the sun brings trouble, pain, and eventual disappointment. Chasing happiness through worldly projects feels like trying to catch a gust of wind.

Solomon comes to hate all his hard labor because death will force him to leave every building, garden, and treasure behind. He cannot take a single coin or palace into the grave with him. Everything he spent a lifetime creating will soon belong entirely to someone else.

A builder has no guarantee whether the person who inherits his wealth will manage it wisely or ruin it through pure foolishness. Regardless of his character, that heir will have full control over everything built with skill and sweat. Solomon saw the vanity of pouring his life into an inheritance that a foolish successor could quickly squander.

Realizing that his life's work would pass to uncertain hands, Solomon lets his heart give up on worldly ambition. He stops expecting earthly labor to provide lasting contentment or permanent security. Giving up this false hope felt like a painful defeat for his pride.

A skilled person may spend decades working honestly with wisdom, knowledge, and competence to build an estate. Yet when he dies, all that wealth is handed over to an heir who never lifted a finger to earn it. Solomon calls this imbalance a deep frustration and a great earthly evil.

Solomon asks what a person truly gains from all the stress, anxiety, and endless striving of daily work. If death takes everything away and leaves the worker with nothing in eternity, all that exhausting toil seems meaningless. The question reminds the reader that worldly effort cannot satisfy the eternal soul.

Those who live only for worldly gain spend their daylight hours burdened with stress, conflict, and exhausting problems. Even at night, when the body needs sleep, the mind continues to toss and turn over business worries and plans. Living as a slave to earthly ambition robs a person of both daily joy and nightly rest.

Since hoarding wealth brings only misery, the best practical approach is to enjoy ordinary meals and find honest satisfaction in one's daily work. Solomon recognizes that the ability to actually enjoy simple blessings is a gracious gift from the hand of God. Without God's favor, even the richest feasts cannot bring true peace.

differ.view: Believers are taught that work was given before the Fall as a holy calling, and finding joy in honest labor is a creational gift from God to be received with thanksgiving rather than merely making the best of a bad situation.
Some emphasize that Ecclesiastes issues a positive, God-centered command to pursue joy and delight in simple gifts in the midst of life's mysteries, rather than expressing resigned defeat.

notes.meaning: No one had more food, riches, or chances to enjoy physical life than Solomon did. Yet his experience showed that no human being can truly relish life's gifts without God's blessing. Pure enjoyment does not come from things themselves; it comes only from the Creator.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Greek and Syriac translations read 'apart from Him' rather than the traditional Hebrew reading 'more than I,' emphasizing that no one can find true enjoyment without God's enablement.

notes.meaning: God gives wisdom, understanding, and heartfelt joy to the person who walks faithfully before Him. In contrast, the ungodly person is trapped in the wearisome task of gathering wealth that eventually ends up in the hands of the righteous. For the sinner who leaves God out of his life, all his hard work ends up being empty and like chasing the wind.
